name: Motonormativity
statement: People judge a harm caused by driving more leniently than the same harm from any other source, and the gap survives changing only the words.
meaning: The claim is about judgement, not about driving. Walker, Tapp and Davis wrote five statements about motoring and five parallel statements in which one or two words moved the subject to a non-motoring domain. Leaving a car in the street became leaving belongings in the street; driving in a populated area became smoking in one. The underlying principle in each pair is the same, so anyone applying a general rule should answer both versions alike. Respondents did not. The authors read this as a shared cultural schema in which motoring is treated as normal and proper, so its harms are judged as inevitable and its costs as somebody else's to absorb. Their stronger claim is that the same schema shapes policy and medicine, which is why they framed it as a public health problem rather than a curiosity about survey wording.

origin.who: Ian Walker, Alan Tapp and Adrian Davis
origin.where: International Journal of Environment and Health
origin.note: The paper coined the name and appeared in volume 11, issue 1, pages 21 to 33. Its data are older than its date: YouGov administered the questions on 12 and 13 October 2016. The authors posted a preprint on 14 December 2022, and its repository record is titled 'Motornomativity'. The document itself spells the word correctly, so the slip belongs to the record rather than to the paper.

evidence: 2157 UK adults answered, 1053 given the motoring form of the questionnaire and 1104 the non-motoring form. Four of the five pairs produced different response patterns across forms. The fumes pair was the widest: 17% agreed that people should not drive in populated areas where others breathe the car fumes, against 75% for the same sentence about cigarette fumes, χ2(1) = 671.11, p < .001, φ = .64. The theft pair gave φ = .53, the risk pair φ = .35 and the drive-less pair φ = .23. The fifth pair, on whether a delivery driver or a chef may bend a few rules to stay profitable, showed no difference at all, χ2(1) = 1.45, p = .23, φ = .03. Drivers and non-drivers answered the non-motoring questions almost identically, and differed on only two of the motoring ones, including 18.0% against 31.4% agreement on the driving fumes item. Overall agreement percentages for the other four pairs appear only in the paper's Figure 1, which carries no text layer. Its prose gives percentages for those pairs only split by sex or by social grade. These figures were read off the authors' December 2022 preprint, which is open. The journal version was still closed on 21 September 2026, and its abstract, read at the publisher's own article page that day, carries the same sample size and the same 17% and 75%.

replication.headline: The gap reappeared in an American sample, in a second British poll and in a three-country study, was smallest in the Netherlands, and a Canadian survey found the same asymmetry over speed limits.
replication.detail: Goddard ran the closest thing to a direct repeat, recruiting 403 US adults through Prolific and assigning them at random to the car form (n = 214) or the non-car form (n = 187). Her t-tests on the five-point ratings found all five pairs significant in the pro-car direction, the delivery driver against the chef included, t = 2.95, p = 0.045. That pair fell away only after she dropped the neutral answers and collapsed the rest into agree and disagree, χ2 = 1.531, p = 0.216, which is the test on which it matches the UK null. Her wording for the pair also differs from Walker's, since her delivery driver bends traffic rules to arrive on time rather than health and safety rules to stay profitable. On the fumes item Goddard reports nearly 94% agreeing that people should not expose others to secondhand smoke and fewer than 20% agreeing the equivalent about car exhaust. Walker and te Brömmelstroet then ran 2035 people in the Netherlands, the UK and the USA, and switched to a within-participants design in which everyone rated both halves of each pair. On the fumes pair the mean difference was 2.15 points on their seven-point scale. Their footnote re-scales the 1.60-point gap from the 2016 UK data to 2.24 on a seven-point scale, and both figures are theirs rather than the 2023 paper's. Dutch respondents scored lower on the paper's latent motonormativity measure than British or American ones, both p < 0.001, while the UK and USA did not differ, p = 0.55. A fourth reading comes from a policy institute rather than a journal: Frost and Singer Hobbs polled 2,041 British adults for the Institute for Public Policy Research in December 2023, and reported 73% for the smoking statement, 77% for a loud music statement and 12% for the driving one. The figure carrying those numbers defines them as net scores, agreement minus disagreement, although the report's own prose calls them agreement. The 2025 study borrowed that loud music pair from the same report. A fifth reading tests the asymmetry on a different question. De Sousa and colleagues surveyed 1,532 adults in greater Montreal, assigning 767 to questions about cars and 765 to questions about electric bikes and scooters. The mean speed limit proposed was 26.0 km/h for the light vehicles against 37.6 km/h for cars, p < 0.001, although the authors calculate that a car at its limit carries about 24 times the kinetic energy. Among respondents who wanted a limit, 88.2% of the light vehicle group said danger to others mattered, against 61.4% of the car group. That study swaps the vehicle rather than a word in a sentence, so it extends the finding rather than repeating the design.

study.cite: Walker, I., & te Brömmelstroet, M. (2025). Why do cars get a free ride? The social-ecological roots of motonormativity. Global Environmental Change, 91, 102980.

limits: The five original questions were picked to work. Walker, Tapp and Davis say so, writing that they used questions they felt would stand a good chance of showing a difference, and arguing that ease of elicitation is itself an index of a bias rather than a flaw in the test. The 2025 study describes its own five pairs as chosen somewhat arbitrarily and reports that they hung together poorly, Cronbach α = 0.28, with the authors stating they do not claim to have used the ideal set of items. Removing each subscale in turn did not change their conclusions. Their five mean differences run 2.15 for the fumes pair, 0.39 for loud music, -0.43 for whether traffic or disease deaths can be prevented, -0.29 for whether drivers or machine operators should answer for harm, and -0.91 for subsidising drivers or cyclists, so the effect is not uniform across the topics anyone might test. Jakub Sliačan and Matej Cíbik argue in a 2026 preprint that the whole design rests on the two statements in a pair invoking the same values, and that a difference shows bias only if they do. They say plainly that they are not questioning the data. Everything measured here is agreement with a sentence. Goddard notes that how these norms translate into behaviour or into support for policy is still to be studied. The samples behind the two later studies came from Prolific. Goddard calls hers representative of the US population by age, gender and ethnicity, while the 2025 paper states its samples were not representative of their countries. Goddard's group sizes of 214 and 187 sum to 401, not the 403 participants the paper reports, and her percentages of 53.4 and 46.6 are shares of 401.
misreadings: The 75% against 17% comparison is quoted as though it described the survey. It describes one pair of five. The other three significant pairs gave φ between .23 and .53, and the fifth gave nothing. Popular coverage also treats this as a fact about drivers, when the UK data show non-drivers answering the non-motoring questions much as drivers did, which is what led the authors to argue that non-drivers have absorbed the majority view. Calling it an unconscious bias suggests an implicit measure, and no reaction-time or association test is involved: the evidence is agreement with statements. The framing of motonormativity as a discovery of 2023 also hides the collection date, which is October 2016. Ian Walker is an author of the 2023 paper and of the 2025 one, so the three-country study is a repeat by an original author. Goddard, the IPPR poll and the Montreal survey are the outside readings.

sources.text: Walker, I., Tapp, A., & Davis, A. (2023). Motonormativity: how social norms hide a major public health hazard. International Journal of Environment and Health, 11(1), 21-33. Not obtained on 21 September 2026. The publisher sells the full text, and its free article page, read that day, carries the abstract, the authors, the volume and the page range. Unpaywall lists the UWE Bristol repository copy as the submitted version, and that host answered a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall, so no open copy of the version of record was found.

Walker, I., Tapp, A., & Davis, A. (2022). Motornomativity: How social norms hide a major public health hazard. Preprint, posted 14 December 2022. Read in full, downloaded from the repository's own file route. Its title page says it is to be published in the journal above, and every statistic on this page was taken from it rather than from the journal version.

Goddard, T. (2024). Windshield bias, car brain, motornormativity: different names, same obscured public health hazard. Findings, August 2024. Read in full from the publisher's open access PDF. Its Table 1 carries the t-tests and its Table 2 the collapsed chi-square tests, which disagree about the delivery driver pair.

Walker, I., & te Brömmelstroet, M. (2025). Why do cars get a free ride? The social-ecological roots of motonormativity. Global Environmental Change, 91, 102980. Read in full as the published version of record, which the University of Amsterdam repository serves openly under a Creative Commons licence after the publisher refused the request. Its Table 2 holds the five mean differences and its first footnote the re-scaling of the 2016 figure.

Frost, S., & Singer Hobbs, M. (2024). Who gets a good deal? Revealing public attitudes to transport in Great Britain. Institute for Public Policy Research, April 2024. Read in full as the institute's own open PDF. Its Figure 2.6 defines the three transport percentages as net scores, and its footnote dates the polling to December 2023.

de Sousa, J., Vinet, A., Chabot, F., Zhang, X., & Waygood, O. (2026). Motonormativity and speed limits. Findings, ahead of print, 12 March 2026. Read in full from the publisher's open access PDF. The source of the Montreal sample sizes and of the two mean speed limits.

Sliačan, J., & Cíbik, M. (2026). Systemic motonormativity. SocArXiv preprint, posted 25 June 2026. Read in full from the repository's own file route, and not peer reviewed. The source of the objection that the design assumes each pair of statements invokes the same values.
